level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2 is true. Right rule: A double is an approximation: Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) is 2.0000000000000004, so the == test is false; compare doubles with a tolerance.

wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double, whatever its value: 207. is 207.0 and 2.3e4 is 23000.0, so int n = 2.3e4; does not compile.

Points to LT (at each operator the narrower operand is promoted, then the operation is done in double and rounded). Applied unevenly: the student promotes to double on one line but keeps integer division on another, e.g. treats 1/2 * x as 0.5 * x on one pass and as 0 on the next. (here mixing in: "Math.sqrt(2) * Math.sqrt(2) == 2 is true")

Changing a variable from int to double changes / from truncating to real division and changes the printed form (3 becomes 3.0); changing back needs a cast and loses the fraction. Invariant: values are approximations, so reordering a sum ((a+b)+c vs a+(b+c)) may change the last digits.
wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (int t = 0; t < T; t++) makes exactly T moves; with <= it makes T + 1, while the ranks are still divided by T.

wrong rule: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. Right rule: A simulation only estimates the ranks: about 10^n moves for n-digit precision, tens of thousands of moves for two accurate places and millions for three.

Applies LT (draw r, find next page, then freq[page]++) unevenly: e.g. counting the current page before the move on some passes, or resetting sum only on the first pass. (here mixing in: "< vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable")

wrong rule: A variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: r and sum are declared inside the t-loop body and are created anew on every move; freq and page must be declared before the loop to persist.

Changing the start page keeps the limit (mixing); increasing T keeps the estimates but makes them more accurate (about 10x moves per extra digit); changing < to <= or the division by T breaks the normalisation.
wrong rule: The body of a for statement executes at most once. Right rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times.

wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. Right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.

wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. Right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.

wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. Right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.
wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. Right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.

wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. Right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). Right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

Applies the for sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: updates before the body on the first pass only, re-runs the init after a pass, or skips the test on some passes. (here mixing in: "The body of a for statement executes at most once")

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).
wrong rule: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. Right rule: freq[i]/T is only an estimate: about 10^n moves for n-digit precision and many more for accuracy.

wrong rule: A result printed with many decimal places must be accurate to those places. Right rule: Printing %8.5f does not make the estimate accurate to 5 places; ensuring accuracy is often the hardest part.

Applies LT (increment after each move, divide by T after the loop) unevenly: e.g. incrementing the page before the move on some passes, or dividing inside the loop. (here mixing in: "A short simulation gives the exact page ranks")
Invariant: the counts sum to T, so the fractions sum to 1; dividing before casting ((double)(freq[i] / T)) or counting outside the loop breaks it.

wrong rule: The cumulative-probability boundary test is inclusive/exclusive interchangeably. Right rule: Add p[page][j] to sum first and then test r < sum; sum is the right endpoint of interval j, so r lands in interval j with probability equal to its length.

Applies LT (r drawn once; for each j: add p[page][j] to sum, then test r < sum) unevenly: e.g. testing before adding on some passes, or drawing a new r for each j. (here mixing in: "the cumulative-probability boundary test is inclusive/exclusive interchangeably")

Changing the search (linear to binary) or the order of pages keeps the distribution of outcomes; replacing r < sum with r <= sum changes it only on a zero-probability event; moving Math.random() into the loop breaks it.

wrong rule: A 2-D array is one thing, not an array of arrays. Right rule: Java represents p[][] as an array of N row arrays; p[page] is itself a 1-D double array (the distribution used by the random move).

wrong rule: Multi-dimensional arrays must be rectangular. Right rule: Each row is its own array, so rows can differ in length (a ragged array); the transition matrix is created square with new double[N][N].
wrong rule: A page with no outgoing links can have an all-zero row. Right rule: Every row must be a probability distribution summing to 1; a page with no links gets 1/N in every column.

wrong rule: The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from. Right rule: For the random-surfer chain the long-run probabilities are the same for all starting pages (basic limit theorem); that is why RandomSurfer can start at page 0.

Applies LT (each step uses the row of the current state) unevenly: e.g. on some steps using the starting page's row instead of the current page's row. (here mixing in: "The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from")
Changing the start state keeps the limiting distribution (if the chain mixes); removing the random leap can break mixing; squaring the matrix gives two-step probabilities.

wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

wrong rule: Java has no long literals. Right rule: An integer literal ending in L is a long.
wrong rule: 207. and 2.3e4 are int values because they are whole numbers. Right rule: A decimal point or scientific notation makes the literal a double.
